# Lime burning and lime mortar (`lime_burning`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: Limestone, chalk or shells held at a bright red heat (about 900 °C) for a day or more lose 44 % of their weight as gas and become quicklime. Quicklime takes up water with violent heat and falls to slaked lime, which is kept as a putty under water. One part lime putty to about three parts sharp sand makes mortar; it hardens slowly by taking carbon dioxide back from the air and turning to limestone again. Lime also makes lye caustic, loosens hair from hides, sweetens sour soil, whitewashes and disinfects.
- Pitfalls:
  - Quicklime burns skin and blinds; slaking a large heap can boil over and set wood alight. Wet quicklime in a ship or cart can start a fire.
  - Underburnt cores stay stone; overburnt lime slakes late and pops out of the plaster.
  - Ordinary lime mortar does not set under water or in thick, airless masses.
  - Using sea sand or dirty, loamy sand; the mortar stays weak and damp.
  - Burning gypsum is a different, much cooler process (about 150 °C) and gives plaster, not lime.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 7500 BC – lime plaster floors and statues in the Levant ('Ain Ghazal); c. 2500 BC lime kilns in Mesopotamia; egypt: pharaonic building used mainly gypsum plaster; lime mortar becomes common under the Ptolemies; india: c. 2600 BC – lime and gypsum plaster at Indus cities; china: c. 3rd millennium BC – lime-plastered floors; by c. 5th c. AD sticky-rice lime mortar; greece: by c. 1500 BC – lime plaster in Minoan and Mycenaean building; rome: c. 160 BC – Cato describes a lime kiln; Vitruvius gives mortar proportions; americas: c. 1000 BC onwards – Maya burn limestone for plaster, stucco and for treating maize
- Read:
  - Cato the Elder, De agri cultura 38
  - Vitruvius, De architectura II.5
  - Norman Davey, A History of Building Materials (1961)
